title: Tributes for ‘man who moved markets’
full_text:
Even inflation showed a moment of respect to legendary former Westpac chief economist Bill Evans. There was a surprise cooling in the quarterly inflation data, the numbers coming hours after the veteran economist had died.
Mr Evans lost his long battle with cancer on Tuesday night, surrounded by family at Melbourne’s Alfred Hospital. He died on his 76th birthday.
Mr Evans signed off from a career of more than four decades as Westpac’s chief economist two years ago, handing over the role to former Reserve Bank assistant governor Luci Ellis.
He was widely regarded as the nation’s leading market economist, and one of the most accurate when it came to Reserve Bank interest rate calls – often by breaking ranks with the economic pack.
Mr Evans’ insights helped shape economic policy over the decades and he briefed politicians just as much as he was also counsel to successive Westpac boards and management about the financial landscape, including chief executives Bob Joss, David Morgan and Gail Kelly. He was known for his laconic style and as a person who made the darker corners of economics accessible to many.
“For so long Bill was such a big part of the way Australians understand and think about our economy and he’ll be badly missed,” said Jim Chalmers, who paid tribute on Wednesday.
“I never left a conversation with Bill without a new insight or a deeper understanding.” Mr Evans’ longevity in economics gave him unrivalled perspective as he helped make sense of repeated shocks, including the global financial crisis, the dotcom crash, the mining supercycle and later the near zero interest rate policy of the Covid pandemic.
“Bill was a once-in-a-generation talent and one of Australia’s most respected and influential economists,” Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller said.
“Known to many as the man who moves markets, over three decades he helped guide Westpac and its customers through every economic cycle.” Mr Miller said Mr Evans’ insights were like “gold dust” – not only for the business world but for governments, journalists, investors and households.
“He knew everything about the economy but he would always explain things in a way that everyone could understand. That’s a rare gift,” Mr Miller said. “Bill leaves an extraordinary legacy. His influence on Westpac and on Australia’s economic community will endure for many years to come. We will miss him dearly.” One of Mr Evans’ biggest calls was in mid-2011, when he predicted cash rates would start to be cut, when much of the market was tipping rate rises. The call proved correct later that year as the central bank started on its decade-long rate cutting cycle.
His views on the economy became the trusted voice coming out of the pandemic. Even on his retirement two years ago, Mr Evans was warning that the RBA needed to “strengthen the rhetoric” on inflation in order to head off a potential price-wage spiral.
The prevailing view at the time was the worst of inflation was behind us, which would clear the way for deeper interest rate cuts. Since then the RBA has dramatically reversed course, raising rates three times.
